background_notes.justification: A compact subset of the Hausdorff Euclidean space is closed, so its complement is open. Each boundary point of the closed box has a coordinate ±R and cannot belong to C. Thus that open complement is the required neighborhood, on which both factors, hence g, vanish.

background_notes.fact: The slice derivative d(s)=∂j g(Phi(y,s)) is interval-integrable on [-R,R]. Since -R<R, oriented integration from -R to R equals restricted integration over [-R,R].

background_notes.justification: A continuous scalar function on a compact interval is Borel measurable and bounded, say by B; its absolute integral is bounded by B times the finite interval length 2R. The derivative is continuous by smoothness and composition with Phi, so this applies to each fixed slice. Oriented interval integration has positive orientation for -R<R; adding or removing the two endpoints changes no Lebesgue integral because singletons have measure zero.

background_notes.justification: On Borel coordinate rectangles the pushforward product measure has the product of the side lengths, equal to Euclidean Lebesgue measure. Bounded half-open rectangles form a generating intersection-stable family with a countable finite-measure cover, so uniqueness of sigma-finite measures gives equality on Borel sets. Phi maps the product box bijectively onto Q. The integrands and boxes here are Borel, so passing to completed Lebesgue measures does not change their integrals; no assertion identifying every completed product sigma algebra is needed. For n=1, the map is the identity after deleting the singleton factor and its mass is 1.

background_notes.justification: For an integrable function zero off Q, multiplication by 1_Q leaves it unchanged, and integration against restricted measure equals integration of that product. Linearity applies to the two integrable summands. Symmetry of a real Euclidean dot product follows termwise from commutativity of real multiplication; thus reversing its factors gives the identical integrable scalar function.

background_notes.justification: On the compact product box w is continuous and has a finite bound B. It is Borel measurable, and the product measure is supported on that box with mass (2R)^(n-1)(2R)<∞, where the exponent-zero factor is 1. Its absolute integral is at most B times that mass. Finite measures are s-finite, since each is already one finite measure.
